newsitem.title: USA: U.S. proposes changes in minority contracts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. proposes changes in minority contracts.

text.p: The Justice Department said on Tuesday it will publish proposed regulations changing affirmative action programmes that give blacks and other minorities preferences for federal government contracts.

Department officials descibed it as another step under President Bill Clinton's pledge to "mend not end" affirmative action after a landmark 1995 Supreme Court ruling making it harder for the government to set aside contracts for minority businesses.
They said the proposed regulations, to be published on Friday, were virtually the same as what the Justice Department had recommended and announced in May.
Final rules are expected to be ready in the fall, with the changes then going into operation, the officials said.
"The proposed regulation is comprehensive. It will affect the contracting practices of every executive branch agency," one official said.
Minority contracts now represent about 6 percent of total government purchases. The officials said the proposed changes would not necessarily lead to a decrease.
The proposed regulations modify the way in which the government can use race-based affirmative action in purchasing goods and services from contractors.

The proposal sets up a process to determine the level of minority contracting that would exist in a specific industry without the effects of discrimination. If the actual minority contracting is below that benchmark level for 80 various industries, affirmative action steps would be allowed.

The officials said the department has concluded that affirmative action in federal procurement still was needed to help break down discriminatory barriers that hurt contracting opportunities for minority-owned businesses.
"The administration remains convinced that carefully tailored affirmative action measures remain essential to overcoming the effects of past and continuing discrimination," one official said.
